questions.stem: A student places a plotting compass at different positions around a bar magnet and records the direction the compass needle points. At which location would the compass needle point directly AWAY from the magnet's north pole?

options.text: Near the south pole of the magnet
Along the side of the magnet, midway between the poles
Directly beyond the north pole, along the axis of the magnet
At the exact centre of the magnet

questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines emerge from the north pole and loop around to enter the south pole. A compass needle aligns with the field direction, so directly beyond the north pole it points away from it (outward along the axis). Near the south pole (A), the needle would point toward the magnet. Along the side (B), it would curve. At the centre (D), the field runs from south to north inside the magnet.

questions.stem: A steel paperclip and a copper coin are both brought near a strong bar magnet. Which statement correctly describes what happens?

options.text: Both are attracted to the magnet because all metals are magnetic
The paperclip is attracted but the copper coin is not, because only iron, cobalt, nickel, and steel are magnetic materials
Neither is attracted because only other magnets can interact with a bar magnet
The copper coin is attracted but the paperclip is repelled

questions.explanation: Only iron, cobalt, nickel, and steel (an alloy containing iron) are magnetic materials. A steel paperclip is attracted to a magnet. Copper is not a magnetic material, so the coin is not attracted. A common misconception (A) is that all metals are magnetic, but most metals (aluminium, copper, gold, silver) are not.

questions.stem: Two bar magnets are placed end to end on a table. Magnet A has its north pole facing Magnet B's north pole. The magnets are 5 cm apart. If the distance is reduced to 2.5 cm, what happens to the force between them?

options.text: The repulsive force stays the same
The repulsive force decreases
The force changes from repulsive to attractive
The repulsive force increases

questions.explanation: Like poles (north-north) repel each other. The magnetic force increases as the distance between the poles decreases. Halving the distance significantly increases the repulsive force. The force does not change direction (C) -- like poles always repel regardless of distance. The force cannot stay the same (A) or decrease (B) when the magnets are brought closer.

questions.stem: A student breaks a bar magnet in half, hoping to isolate a single north pole. What does the student actually get?

options.text: One piece that is a north pole only and one piece that is a south pole only
Two pieces that are no longer magnetic
Two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south pole
One magnetic piece and one non-magnetic piece

questions.explanation: Magnetic poles always exist in pairs -- you can never isolate a single pole. When a magnet is broken in half, each piece becomes a complete magnet with its own north and south pole. This is because magnetism arises from the alignment of atomic magnetic domains throughout the material, so every fragment retains both poles.

questions.stem: The magnetic field strength at a point near a magnet is 0.04 T. A second measurement is taken further from the magnet where the field lines are spaced twice as far apart. Which value best represents the field strength at the second point?
questions.explanation: The spacing of magnetic field lines indicates the field strength. Where field lines are closer together, the field is stronger; where they are further apart, the field is weaker. If the lines are spaced twice as far apart, the field strength is approximately half: 0.04 T / 2 = 0.02 T. A common error is thinking wider spacing means a stronger field (A), but it is the opposite.
